cues.text: Welcome to the Plant Physiology evidence workshop.
A leaf chamber records net carbon dioxide uptake of eight micromoles per
square
metre per second in light.
A separate dark measurement records carbon dioxide release of two in the same
units.
If the question asks us to assume the same respiratory loss in light,
estimated
gross uptake is ten.
The chamber measures a net exchange, not every internal carbon reaction
separately.
Respiration does not stop when a leaf is illuminated.
However, dark respiration is not automatically an exact measurement of
respiration in light.
Write the supplied approximation before adding the rates, and keep area, time
and gas units consistent.
A light response graph usually rises from negative net carbon uptake in
darkness.
The light compensation point is where net uptake reaches zero: photosynthetic
uptake balances respiratory release under those conditions.
It does not mean both processes have stopped.
At higher light, the graph may flatten.
Increasing light alone then produces little additional net uptake, suggesting
that another process or resource limits the measured rate.
It does not prove which factor is limiting.
Compare carbon dioxide, temperature and water status while controlling other
variables.
A temperature rise caused by the lamp can confound a light intensity
experiment.
Read the horizontal and vertical axes before identifying a compensation point
or plateau.
Separate location, energy and carbon sources.
In the chloroplast, thylakoid reactions use light to drive electron transfer
and support ATP and NADPH formation.
Oxygen released in oxygenic photosynthesis comes from water.
The Calvin cycle operates in the stroma and incorporates carbon dioxide into
organic molecules using ATP and NADPH.
Calling it light independent means the fixation steps do not directly require
photons.
It does not mean the cycle normally runs only at night, or that it is
independent of products and regulation linked to light.
An isotope label question must say which molecule is labelled and which
product
is tested.
Do not infer the oxygen source merely from the balanced overall equation.
Use a net carbon budget rather than counting every intermediate as an exported
product.
In the standard Calvin cycle accounting, fixation of three carbon dioxide
molecules yields one net three carbon glyceraldehyde three phosphate, or G
three P, while the remaining carbon regenerates the acceptor.
The cycle consumes nine ATP and six NADPH for that net product.
A six carbon carbohydrate equivalent therefore corresponds to six carbon
dioxide, eighteen ATP and twelve NADPH in this simplified accounting.
It is not correct to claim that each individual turn immediately releases a
glucose molecule.
These figures describe the Calvin cycle itself; additional cellular synthesis
and transport can have other costs.
In the standard C four pathway, initial fixation uses phosphoenolpyruvate
carboxylase in mesophyll cells, producing four carbon acids.
Their processing supplies carbon dioxide around Rubisco in bundle sheath
cells,
reducing the oxygenation reaction under suitable conditions.
The Calvin cycle still fixes carbon through Rubisco.
C four concentration has an additional energy cost, so do not label it
universally superior under every environment.
High temperature, bright light and conditions favouring photorespiration can
make the concentration mechanism advantageous.
When interpreting a comparison, ask whether temperature, carbon dioxide and
water availability were controlled.
A single faster leaf measurement does not establish that every C four species
always outperforms every C three species.
For one glucose molecule, glycolysis in the cytosol produces two pyruvate
molecules.
Four ATP are formed during the payoff reactions, but two were invested
earlier,
so the net yield is two ATP.
Two NADH are also produced per glucose in the standard pathway.
A question asking gross ATP formation therefore has a different answer from
one
asking net ATP gain.
Glycolysis does not directly consume oxygen.
Sustained operation nevertheless requires regeneration of oxidised NAD, either
through aerobic metabolism or fermentation pathways under the appropriate
conditions.
Avoid giving a universal total ATP yield for complete respiration without
knowing the accounting assumptions.
Here we are counting glycolysis only, not the citric acid cycle or oxidative
phosphorylation.
Respiratory quotient is carbon dioxide released divided by oxygen consumed.
If a sample releases six millilitres of carbon dioxide while consuming eight
millilitres of oxygen, measured under matching conditions over the same
interval, the quotient is zero point seven five.
Complete carbohydrate oxidation has a theoretical quotient of one, whereas
lipid oxidation commonly has a quotient below one.
A measured intermediate value does not uniquely identify a substrate:
mixtures,
measurement conditions and additional metabolism can affect it.
If oxygen consumption is zero, this ratio has a zero denominator and is not an
ordinary finite quotient.
Never divide carbon dioxide volume by an oxygen rate unless the units and
observation period are reconciled first.
Two seedlings each gain two grams of dry mass in five days.
Their average absolute growth rates are equal, at zero point four grams per
day.
If their starting masses differ, their relative growth need not be equal.
For positive measured masses, the mean relative rate over an interval can be
calculated as the change in natural logarithm of mass divided by elapsed time.
A seedling growing from two to four grams doubles, while one growing from ten
to twelve does not.
Compare treatment effects using matched starting material and replicated
groups.
Fresh mass can change because of water content, so define whether the outcome
is length, fresh mass, dry mass or another measure before interpreting growth.
